keritot-13b-13-14.note: Rav Aḥa of Huzal had taken a vow forbidding himself any benefit from his wife, and came to Rav Ashi to have it dissolved. Rav Ashi told him to go and come back tomorrow, because he had drunk wine, and pointed out that Rav would not give public lectures on a Festival day because of drunkenness. Rav Aḥa objected that Rav ruled like Rabbi Elazar, and Rav Ashi mixed water into his wine. Rav Ashi answered that Rabbi Elazar's ruling covers a quarter-log of wine, and he had drunk more than that.
keritot-13b-13-14.why: The Gemara has just cited Rav's ruling that the law follows Rabbi Elazar, who exempts a priest who drank diluted wine. This incident tests how far that ruling reaches for a Sage asked to rule after drinking; the discussion then lists what may not be taught after wine.

keritot-28a-30-31.note: The Temple courtyard cried out four times: to remove Ḥofni and Pineḥas, sons of Eli, for making the Sanctuary impure; to open for Yoḥanan ben Nedavai, who ate so much that no sacrificial meat was ever left over; to let Elishama ben Pikai in as High Priest; and to expel Yissakhar from the village of Barkai, who wrapped his hands in silk to do the service. King Yannai and the queen asked this High Priest whether goat or lamb was better. He said that if goat were better it would be the daily offering, gesturing with his hand. The king ordered his right hand cut off; he bribed the official and lost his left, and the king had the right cut off too. Rav Yosef blessed God for this retribution.
keritot-28a-30-31.why: The mishna teaches that although lambs are usually listed before goats in the Torah, the two are equal. Right after the story, Rav Ashi and Ravina say Yissakhar's answer shows he had not learned this mishna, or even read the Torah's verses.
